title: Synchronizing evolving rep range with movement patterns, variations & rotations
summary: NH explains how to match evolving rep ranges to specific lifts: protect fragile structures like the biceps with moderate ranges, push compounds like the deadlift into heavy ranges, and keep partials high-rep. Each lift gets its own rep range, days should mix intensity and volume, and rotated lifts must replace the 'ghost tonnage' of the lift they replace.
claims: No body part needs a special intensity or volume zone; NH's enlarged striking zone is 2-15 reps for every muscle
Most of a program's tonnage should sit at 4-8 or 4-10 reps, up to 4-12, with high-volume outliers and some heavier movements
Evolving rep ranges change volume and intensity constantly; going from 2 to 10 reps is more than four times the tonnage of the first set
Higher-intensity sets in an evolving range should be used to add weight so progressive overload never stops
Movements hard on tendons or on muscles with weaker structural integrity should skew toward the volume end
No 2-5 rep ranges for biceps; injuries usually occur when the negative reverses into the positive and the biceps tendon is fragile
For biceps NH uses a minimum of 4 reps up to 12
Protecting the biceps doesn't mean only high volume; never pushing intensity leads to junk volume
Compound movements benefit most from high intensity because many joints share the load, though form breakdown must still be avoided
NH can do 2-rep maxes on the deadlift with zero lower back pain and sees more progress there than on any other lift
Don't do 12-rep maxes on conventional deadlifts; cardiovascular endurance and structural integrity limit you more than muscle
Keep the deadlift around 2-5 reps and the squat around 3-8 or 3-6
Use partials for high reps, not to move very heavy weight
A rep range is married to a lift; decide each lift's rep range before placing it in a day, and expect variations to need different ranges
NH opposes intensity days and volume days; each day should mix both because intensity drives progression and volume drives tonnage
NH does all his low-rep strength work as the workout opener and the rest as volume, because he has good work capacity and returns to baseline well
Some people need two intensity-focused movements and one volume movement; NH does one intensity and two or three volume
When a strength set is at its heaviest, the following volume work should be at its lowest intensity so tonnage complements rather than competes
Within an evolving range you choose the progression, e.g. aiming for 6 reps after 5 last week, so you can also mismanage it and punish yourself
Pairing 3x3-5 heavy deadlifts with RDLs for 8-12 on the same day is wasteful because it is the same movement
Tonnage accumulation doesn't mean doing as many movements as possible for one muscle; work it until your ability to return to baseline is shot
In a rotation, a lift's tonnage is replaced, not added; a lighter rotated lift like the RDL needs more reps to fill the 'ghost tonnage'
Ghost tonnage must be replaced by a movement targeting similar muscles; picking a completely different movement makes it a different day
